questions.q: Per this lesson, what can go wrong with a documentation set even when every individual diagram in it is technically correct?
options: Nothing — technically correct diagrams are always trustworthy together
Technically correct diagrams cannot be stored in the same document
If different architects use inconsistent shapes, lines, or conventions diagram to diagram, a reader can no longer assume meaning carries over from one diagram to the next
Salesforce blocks documents containing more than one diagram style
questions.explain: Each diagram can be internally correct yet the set as a whole becomes untrustworthy if conventions differ diagram to diagram — a reader can't assume what a shape or line means stays consistent without an agreed standard.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call a missing legend 'the single most common standards failure'?
options: Because legends are required by Salesforce metadata validation rules
Because a legend is only needed for ERDs, never for sequence diagrams
Because legends make diagrams load faster in Schema Builder
Because without a legend, an ambiguous element (like a plain line that could be lookup or master-detail) is only reliably interpretable by the person who drew it
questions.explain: A legend is what turns an ambiguous shape or line into an unambiguous one for any reader, not just the author — without it, a diagram is only fully trustworthy to the person who drew it.

questions.q: Which of these is given as an example of a 'house style' element a documentation set should settle on?
options: A fixed shape vocabulary, so the same shape always means the same kind of thing across every diagram in the set
Using a different shape for 'external system' in every new diagram to keep things visually interesting
Omitting version/date stamps so diagrams look cleaner
Avoiding labels on relationship lines so diagrams stay uncluttered
questions.explain: A house style fixes a shape vocabulary, a color convention, a labeling style, and a version/date stamp so every diagram in the set is consistent — the other three options describe exactly the inconsistency this lesson warns against.

questions.q: What does this lesson point to as a real-world example of a consistent visual convention used across many related diagrams?
options: Random clip-art styles used inconsistently across Trailhead modules
Salesforce's own architect.salesforce.com decision guides, which use a consistent visual vocabulary across dozens of different guides
Each Salesforce release notes PDF, which intentionally varies its diagram style every release
Internal-only documentation that is never shared outside one team
questions.explain: The lesson cites architect.salesforce.com's decision guides as a reference point for consistent notation across many different topics, letting readers move between guides without relearning conventions each time.

questions.q: Per the standards-compliance checklist in this lesson, what does it mean if a reader who has seen one other diagram in a set still cannot correctly interpret a new diagram without asking a clarifying question?
options: The diagram isn't done yet, even if its content is technically accurate, because it has failed the consistency test the checklist is built around
The diagram is finished as long as it's technically accurate
The reader should be removed from the review process
The diagram needs more color, regardless of notation consistency
questions.explain: The checklist's final test is whether a reader familiar with the set's conventions can interpret a new diagram unaided — failing that test means the diagram isn't standards-compliant yet, regardless of its underlying technical accuracy.
